title: Sold! Why live cattle auctions still matter to Alberta ranchers in an era of online bidding
summary: Ranchers say you can still tell when it’s auction day in farming towns: trucks are lined up on the streets, the coffee shops are busy and local commerce surges.

image.caption: Over 2,000 cattle a day can move through the auction mart in Stettler, Alta. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton
Ranchers say you can still tell when it’s auction day in farming towns: trucks are lined up on the streets, the coffee shops are busy and local commerce surges.
Physical auction rings vital for smaller operations and rural communities, producers say

Amidst rapid-fire auction chants and high-stakes bids, cattle lumber through the gates of the auction ring in Stettler, Alta. Trotting in and out in twos and threes, they’re mostly cooperative, though a few stubborn ones keep the handlers hustling.
More than 2,000 head are on the block this crisp day. It’s the thick of the fall run, the annual October-November window when many ranchers bring their spring-born calves to market.

“We'll sell $12-million worth of cattle here today,” says Dave Mailer, owner of the Stettler Auction Mart, a fixture in the central Alberta community since 1953. Standing on a boardwalk above the pens, he raises his voice to be heard over the bawling cattle below.
A calf bawls in a pen at the Stettler Auction Mart, Alta. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

Live auction marts like this one anchor life in rural Alberta, even as online bidding grows in popularity. Ranchers say you can still tell when it’s sale day in farming towns: trucks are lined up on the streets, the coffee shops are busy and local commerce surges.
Mailer says it’s difficult to replace the live floor. “For the customer to be able to see their cattle sell and the customer to buy… [it’s] the best thing.”
Inside the ring, an auctioneer’s rapid-fire chant rolls by in a rhythmic blur: “Two-seventy-five, two-seventy-five,” he prompts, pushing the crowd to beat bids locked at $2.65 and $2.70 a pound.
Stettler Auction Mart owner Dave Mailer, top, auctions off a pair of cattle in the ring as a rancher, bottom left, bids from the stands. (Bob Grieve/CBC)
Decades ago, producers had to ship cattle to stockyards in major cities like Edmonton or Calgary. Over time, independent country markets helped decentralize beef trade in western Canada.
Today, ranchers can browse online catalogues and video clips to buy cattle remotely, or log in to bid live on sale days like this one.

“That's your whole year's paycheque, your whole year's income happening in roughly a few seconds,” says Lance Neilson of a typical auction. He pulled an empty trailer the 30 kilometres from his ranch, hoping to fill it with calves, then return in a few days with a load of heifers to sell.
Physical rings are vital for smaller operators, Neilson says.
“They end up being able to bring 20 calves or 10 calves, or maybe only bring one or two cows. And that gives you options to keep smaller producers in.”
Beef producers Jack and Shirley Neilsen at the Stettler Auction Mart. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

Jack and Shirley Neilsen have raised purebred Simmental cattle for decades, though they recently downsized their herd by about three-quarters. Up in the bleachers, the couple sit side by side, waiting intently for their calves to enter the ring.

“I guess we're people of old habits,” Jack says. “The staff here is very good to us. They know our name, they know us, whereas [at] some of the larger auctions, they don't. We're not just a number, we're a name here.”
For the Neilsens, sale day is woven into the rhythm of rural life.
“Jack, especially, coming in here — [he’ll] have coffee with a lot of the old guys and reminisce and talk about the past and hopefully the future,” Shirley says.
'Tough to beat that live atmosphere'

About 130 kilometres west, in the shadow of the Rocky Mountains near Rimbey, Dan Skeels walks his fourth-generation ranch, checking cattle for signs of pneumonia — a risk at this time of year with warmer days and chilly nights.
Skeels, who is also a world-champion auctioneer, says auction days don't just support ranchers, they fuel entire towns.
Dan Skeels stands on his fourth-generation ranch near Rimbey, Alta. Skeels is a cattle rancher and former world-champion auctioneer. (Nadeer Hashmi/CBC)

“I'm going to use our small town of Rimbey as a prime example. When it's sale day, the community's hustling, it's bustling. There's that much more commerce taking place in the town... It really helps the local economy.”
Skeels says he knows livelihoods are riding on every call he makes as auctioneer.

“I think it's pretty tough to beat that live atmosphere," he says, noting the main advantage is what the industry calls true price discovery — competitive bidding that determines what cattle are actually worth on a given day.
“You may have a producer that we sell their entire calf crop in 10 minutes… So, it's a big job.”
Cattle stand in the ring surrounded by handlers and auctioneers at the auction mart in Stettler, Alta. (Bob Grieve/CBC)
Second year of record prices

Rick Wright, CEO of the Livestock Markets Association of Canada, says online bidding now accounts for about 12 per cent of sales at commercial auction marts, which remain the benchmark for producers to see their livestock's true market value.
“I can sit and watch sales in Alberta, I can watch sales in Kansas, I can watch sales in Ontario, and get a real feel of the real market,” he says.
Ranchers can now preview video livestock listings in an online auction catalogue, then bid remotely during live sales. (Bob Grieve/CBC)
Wright says after a long drought, a second year of record cattle prices is giving much-needed breathing room to cow-calf producers, which make up the largest share of beef farms in Canada.
“They're certainly in a better financial position over the last two years than they have been in the previous five to seven,” he says.
“But their expenses have also gone up — interest has gone up, diesel fuel has gone up. The cost of raising the cattle has gone up by quite a bit.”
A handler moves a small group of cattle through the back pens toward the auction ring in Stettler. (Bob Grieve/CBC)
Back in the Stettler ring, Mailer and his crew are on hour 12 of a marathon sale day, with the bids and the auctioneer’s chant showing no sign of slowing down.
“It's the adrenaline of today,” Mailer says of the rush that keeps them going.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nadeer Hashmi is a reporter for CBC News in Red Deer, Alta. He was formerly a reporter in Yellowknife.
